segments.title: How Age of Sail ratings counted guns
segments.summary: Gun-count labels such as 74 and 80 grouped Age of Sail warships into ratings and gave a concise description of their armament.
segments.body: Labels such as 74 and 80 describe ships by their total number of guns. The approximate bands given here put first rates at 100 guns or more and second rates around 90 guns, or roughly 86 upwards. Third rates run from 84 down to roughly 64 guns. The rating uses gun count as a shorthand for a ship's armament. The comparison with World War II asks why that shorthand lost its value as weapons became more powerful and served different purposes.

evidence.note: The transcript outlines first, second, and third rates by gun totals.

segments.title: Why modern gun totals became misleading
segments.summary: Modern gun totals lost much of their value once calibre, shell effects, range, and accuracy determined what a few weapons could achieve.
segments.body: Individual weapons became much more powerful and specialised. In the hypothetical comparison, a 1930s sloop with at most two or three 4-inch guns could destroy both fleets at the Battle of Trafalgar. Its high-explosive shells and accurate fire at range would make most of the sailing warships single-shot kills in this imagined encounter. The example illustrates how a few modern guns could represent far more combat power than a large Age of Sail total. Counting barrels says little once the weapons and their effects are no longer broadly comparable.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts a 1930s sloop's few modern guns with earlier fleets.

segments.title: Why main-battery calibre matters in a gunnery duel
segments.summary: For a modern warship, its role and principal battery, such as 6-inch or 8-inch cruiser guns, reveal more than a total that mixes many weapon types.
segments.body: A hypothetical World War II ship with 90 guns might have only six 6-inch guns, with the rest of the total including 40 mm weapons, 20 mm weapons, and machine guns. In a ship-to-ship gunnery duel, those six main guns usually provide the most relevant description of its armament. Lighter weapons can take part at very close range or against motor torpedo boats and aircraft, so their importance depends on the opponent and circumstances. Historians therefore identify the ship type and principal calibre, for example a cruiser with 6-inch or 8-inch guns. This longer description preserves distinctions between weapons that a single total would hide.

evidence.note: The transcript distinguishes main 6-inch or 8-inch batteries from lighter weapons and their roles.

segments.title: Why modern warship labels are wordier
segments.summary: A dramatic total such as 90 guns can mislead when many of those weapons are machine guns with little bearing on a ship-to-ship gunnery duel.
segments.body: First-, second-, and third-rate labels were concise. Modern classification needs more words to describe combat capability accurately. The television example asks whether a ship can simply be described as carrying 90 guns. That total hides the fact that roughly 50 could be machine guns, which contribute little to a ship-to-ship gunnery duel. Describing the ship's role and main battery takes more words and keeps the comparison focused on the weapons relevant to that fight.

evidence.note: The transcript explains that a television-friendly total can count about 50 machine guns that do not matter in a ship-to-ship gunnery duel.
